video.title: Shoulder Adduction Will Transform Your Forehand Contact

classification.reason: The coach provides executable instructions including matching your grip to your natural adduction motion without a ball, tilting the torso on low balls to preserve adduction, and practicing the feeling of horizontal adduction during mini tennis.

problem.title_as_question: How Does Shoulder Adduction Create Consistent Forehand Contact?
problem.definition: Forehand contact is fundamentally produced by horizontal shoulder adduction and internal rotation. Without understanding and organizing the stroke around this core contact mechanic, upstream body rotation, speed, and grip choices lead to inconsistent contact and errors.

quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Horizontal shoulder adduction and internal rotation. That is the key. If you can master that, you can master forehand contact.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: The string angle is open or inappropriate at contact when swinging through the ball.
Adding body rotation and swing speed causes more misses rather than a reliable shot.
On low balls, the player cannot execute horizontal shoulder adduction without adjusting body posture.

causes.statement: Contact is produced by closing the shoulder angle (horizontal shoulder adduction), which players often fail to prioritize as the core mechanic.
The arm fails to internally rotate toward the center of the body while horizontally adducting the shoulder.
The racket grip is chosen arbitrarily instead of matching the player's natural and comfortable horizontal shoulder adduction motion.
Upstream elements like torso rotation and swinging faster are added before establishing proper shoulder adduction at contact.
On low balls, the torso fails to tilt and the back knee fails to drop, making it mechanically impossible to adduct the shoulder naturally.

angles.summary: Forehand contact velocity is generated by closing the pectoral-humeral angle with the chest muscles pressing the arm forward.
Players believe torso rotation is mandatory to hit a forehand, but a solid shot can be struck purely through shoulder adduction.
Players throw the racket over their head (reverse finish) when jammed because they seek to preserve that same adduction feeling.

solutions.summary: Perform a comfortable bare-arm adduction motion, place the racket in hand, and check that the grip yields a slightly closed string angle at contact.
solutions.external_goal: Slightly closed string angle at contact position

solutions.summary: Hit shots keeping the chest facing forward and only adducting the shoulder, isolating contact before introducing body rotation.
When the ball is low, tilt the torso and lower the back knee to recreate the comfortable shoulder adduction plane.
In mini tennis, focus purely on feeling horizontal adduction and finding the contact spot out front where it occurs naturally.
solutions.external_goal: Contact spot in front of the body

solutions.summary: Prepare the racket away from your body, adduct your shoulder through the ball, and track it with your eyes the entire time.
